questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
There's only one reason for picking Kyoto: Culture galore! And people don't lie: Even without counting the tourist-favourites like Kinkakuji, Touji, Fushimi Inari, etc., there are so many temples and shrines that I'd wager it's impossible to stand in one single place and not see one.

I also have a few friends that live in the Kansai area, so it seemed like a natural decision to experience the west of Japan on a longer-term scale.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I had no issues. I arrived with a night bus from Tokyo on the day of the orientation, and despite being sleep-deprived and homeless (for one night), it was not a difficult meeting. We even received everything in writing and print, so we could review it when we found a home. Score!

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
There was some general things, such as how to register for classes, how to register for insurances, and how to register for commuter cards. There were many minus-points, such as some, rather far away dormitories not being able to register for commuter cards, and many of the insurances being split-up. Compared to Meiji University or Tokai University, which I have previously exchanged to, there was a lot more to do here.

Also, we were warned with slightly odd choice of words of how to prioritise our time on exchange. One of the international guides even said, "you're here to study, not to have fun," and while the first part may be true, it should be the job of the international coordinators to ensure that the second part doesn't become true.

In any case, the introduction also introduced some poorly-enforced rules of travel: You're not to leave the prefecture during the week, and you're not to leave the country during the active part of a semester. This was an issue for me, who had already arranged a trip to China midway through the semester, and I notified the staff of this immediately. No answer ever arrived, and no trouble ever came of the trip.

I'm trying to say that, despite some very relevant and important information being present in the introductory assistance, it also seems to scare some students away from having a much better exchange than they end up actually having.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I went with a Share House, since properties in the relevant areas for the university are either expensive or run-down. I recommend just going with the dormitory in this case, since it's super close by, and the price was lower than what was originally advertised in the brochures.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
Be aware of what Share House company you pick, and make sure you received the terms of the contract in due time. I was presented with mine on the day of signing, so I didn't have time to ponder whether or not a "50% cut of the deposit goes to the rental company"-clause was fair or not. I ended up spending roughly 9.000 DKK in fees and the like that never came back to me, not in actual rent, nor in cash.

I was living at the Share House 180 Kinkakuji property, and have since heard that Borderless House or Eat Lives Hotel (that is not a hotel) could have been viable options.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
Similar to most other institutions I've been to. One week of trial classes, with a subsequent online registration sheet.

Some of the professors did seem to game this system, however, and one even provided an entirely different exam from the one advertised on the class sheets. She presented this after the selection period had ended.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Each class had their own syllabus sheet, and aside from this, professors seemed helpful.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: There were also lottery classes in this case, but I was succesful in getting all the classes I wanted, at the time when I wanted them.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Ask your professors about the exam type. Most were assignments, which is nicer for an exchange student, but not all.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: BA-level courses that were meant to replace the elective classes offered at UCPH.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I'll be honest and say that I was disappointed at the level of the classes that were taken. Some classes, particularly the ones aimed at International Relations-students, were higher level, but most were conversation classes that presented top-level insight in a range of subjects. That said, some, particularly the ones about the Pacific, were relevant to my field of study.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Arts and Crafts
Dynamism of the Pacific
Language Acquisition
Language Education
Media and Society
Japanese Culture through Field Trips
Security Studies

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
The professors at Language Acquisition and Education were friendly and extremely knowledgeable, and it seemed like the level of the class was artificially adjusted down to help the local students keep up. The Arts and Crafts class was rather difficult to follow, with seemingly no connection between each topic of the class, although the professor was perhaps the most serious of the lot.

Security Studies seemed odd to me, and the professor was very convinced of her own ways. She was the one who decided to use a physical, pen-and-paper essay-style exam with a problem question and 3 hours to write an answer on a large A3 sheet of paper.
She also often quoted "someone" in her slides, and spoke in disconnected ways that made the class difficult to follow. I'm sure I'd have respect for her academics if I read her articles, but I couldn't respect her style of teaching.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Mostly, I got surprised at the abhorrent fees that my Share House company charged me. Of the 5000 DKK deposit, I only received 250 kr. in return, despite leaving the room in pristine condition (no money was charged on account of improper maintenance, an arbitrary cleaning fee and 50% of my deposit was accounted for in the contract). Aside from this, the rental company charged me a late-fee for disclosing my check-out date within a two-month limit - despite having told the company of my length of stay from the beginning.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Transport costs were almost none, since the city is small enough that everyday destinations can be reached by foot. Conversely, the train network is small and not particularly useful, so buses that run irregularly and are often full is the only alternative. I therefore ended up using the rental e-bike service, Luup, more than expected, which drove up my non-regular travel expenses.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Easy access to the clubs (saakuru (circle) in Japanese universities) made it easy to make friends in many different circumstances. I only lightly dabbled in the circles, but many of my international peers made lasting friendships at those.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I don't care much for sports, so I didn't use the university gym, which was free to use. There was a sort of Buddy-system, that did see some of us international students meet with some locals, but this was not often.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I recommend the BBP - Beyond Borders Plaza - for anyone who want to make some local friends. I already knew people there, and I was able to meet even more people there, and even some with whom I was able to meet on their exchange to Denmark.

There is a language exchange program as well, and since Denmark is a surprisingly popular country in Japan, I was able to teach some Danish as well. I wholly recommend engaging in this environment, since it allows a very unfiltered look into the lives of normal university students, who come from all over Japan to study at Ritsumeikan University.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
The mountains to the north of Kyoto are extremely pretty, and renting car with my flatmates and exploring the tight roads and amazing views of these is a fond memory I shan't soon forget.

I took a drivers license for motorcycle while I was away, and since I was able to convert my Danish drivers license to a Japanese one earlier, it was relatively quick and cheap to upgrade it to include motorcycles. The motorcycle industry has been a large part of the post-war economic miracle in Japan, and a motorcycle culture seems deeply imbedded whereever you go, particularly in Kansai, for some reason. There's even a bike temple (Hontakiji) with a friendly Harley-priest. If you meet him, tell him I said hi!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Not particularly difficult, although it is said that Kyoto has a certain irony and unwillingness to point out when you're being rude - so I'm not sure I'll ever know if I was too rude.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
Visit the areas where people are willing to themselves engage with foreigners. Some Japanese, not unlike Danes and indeed most other people, don't want to brave language barriers and endure cultural differences just to talk to a person who will leave the country soon, anyways.

Some do, however, and finding those is much more worthwhile than converting the non-believers.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Hanging out with friends, who invites and when it's appropriate to invite again is difficult.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Quiet and order. And also the drinking culture, being less oriented around clubs and dancing, and more oriented on bars, dinners and singing your heart out at a karaoke.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1: Don't listen to them: Have fun, but also study.
2: Live at the dorm. It seems awesome.
3: If you do live on your own, don't go with Share 180.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: A random tip is to not miss out on becoming part of Coop. It gives you so many discounts on lunches at the university, and it allows you to use the convenience store on campus after-hours. If you don't live in the dorms, there's no explicit reason to sign up, but if you don't do it early, it'll feel like a waste of money by the end. So do it early.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Using the Japanese that I have learned throughout my Japanese study to accomplish the same things that a Japanese person can, and through this, unlock an entirely different side to the conversations I can have with locals. Taking a driving license in the local language, talking to a priest in the local language and getting the feeling that I am not inconvenienced by any language barrier anymore is a freeing feeling - even if there's still a lot of studying to go.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
The fight with my Share House company, which was done in 100% Japanese through emails, since their office is in Nagoya, and they don't bother sending people all the way to Kyoto for petty things like a broken lock, cold showers and disabled wifi (that we're paying for).

Or perhaps it was finally facing the employee that I had been mailing with for weeks, and realising that he is just a normal person, just as he realised that I am just a normal person.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
